role.en: Teacher; central figure of the Gospels

summary.en: Itinerant Jewish teacher and healer of Galilee whose ministry, death and resurrection are the subject of the four Gospels. Crucified under Pontius Pilate at Passover (AD 30 in this atlas's default chronology; AD 33 is also defended).

A Pharisee and Roman citizen from Tarsus in Cilicia who, after a transformative encounter on the Damascus road, became the foremost early Christian missionary, undertaking the journeys mapped here and writing much of the New Testament.

role.en: Companion of Paul on the first journey

summary.en: A Cypriot Levite and early leader of the church who introduced Saul to the apostles and was his senior partner on the first missionary journey, until they parted over John Mark.

role.en: Assistant on the first journey; traditionally the evangelist Mark

summary.en: Travelled with Paul and Barnabas from Antioch but left them at Perga (Acts 13:13); the later disagreement over him split Paul and Barnabas. Traditionally identified with Mark the evangelist.

role.en: Companion of Paul on the second journey

summary.en: A leading member of the Jerusalem church and a Roman citizen who accompanied Paul on the second journey, sharing the Philippian imprisonment.
A young disciple from Lystra, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, who joined Paul on the second journey and became a trusted delegate and the recipient of two letters.
Companion of Paul and author of the Gospel of Luke and Acts; the 'we' passages of Acts (beginning at Troas, Acts 16:10) suggest he joined the journeys as an eyewitness.

Fisherman of Bethsaida/Capernaum and foremost of the Twelve; spokesman at Pentecost and the Jerusalem Council. Strong early tradition places his later ministry and martyrdom at Rome (not directly narrated in Acts).

The proconsul at Paphos who summoned Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:7). Inscriptions attest the senatorial gens Sergia and a 'Paulus [proconsul]' on Cyprus, corroborating the office and family, though none can be tied to the exact official of Acts 13.

Proconsul of Achaia who dismissed the case against Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:12–17). The Delphi (Gallio) inscription dates his proconsulship to c. AD 51–52, the single firmest anchor for Pauline chronology.
The Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to crucifixion. His historicity and title ('prefect') are confirmed by the Pilate Stone found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961.
